claims.text: A two-phase coexistence method using accurate interatomic potentials can reproduce melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on DFT data can provide sufficient accuracy for two-phase coexistence calculations.
The two-phase coexistence method has a much lower computational cost than full ab initio free-energy integration.
Constant-pressure molecular dynamics of a cell containing coexisting solid and liquid phases can be used to determine melting properties.
The equilibrium properties of a solid-liquid interface reflect the balance of free energies between the solid and liquid phases.
At the melting point, coexisting solid and liquid phases are in equilibrium.
Monitoring energy, volume, and structure during solid-liquid coexistence allows the melting temperature to be extracted.
Monitoring solid-liquid coexistence allows the enthalpy of fusion to be extracted.
Monitoring solid-liquid coexistence allows the entropy of fusion to be extracted.
Monitoring solid-liquid coexistence allows the volume change at melting to be extracted.
Direct coexistence bypasses the expensive thermodynamic integrations required by full ab initio free-energy calculations.
Two-phase coexistence results are expected to agree within acceptable uncertainty margins with full ab initio free-energy results.
The reduction in computational expense would make high-throughput melting-property calculations more feasible.
The accuracy of the method depends on the quality of the interatomic potential.
The accuracy of the method may be system-dependent.
Materials with extreme anharmonicity or complex bonding may require additional calibration.
The two-phase coexistence method has been successful in many material systems.
Systematic deviations from full DFT free-energy integration are uncertain for new refractory materials and require system-specific validation.
